papers.abstract: We describe a case of a patient with multiple sclerosis (MS) stable on natalizumab who developed widespread gadolinium-enhancing lesions and clinical relapse seven and eight months after gamma knife radiosurgery (GKRS) for left cerebellar convexity meningioma. We explore how increased blood-brain barrier (BBB) permeability post-GKRS could potentially interfere with the lymphocyte anti-trafficking effect of natalizumab and result in new central nervous system (CNS) inflammation distant from the radiation site. Comprehensive analysis of the patient's chart, brain and spine imaging, serum and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) profiles was conducted. We compiled a graphical representation of treatment changes, radiologic findings, and GKRS initiation within one timeframe. We conducted a structured literature review to support the discussion of this case and hypothesize possible pathophysiological mechanisms contributing to clinical and radiological findings. Seven months after GKRS, follow-up brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) demonstrated multiple gadolinium-enhancing lesions in both cerebral hemispheres, and repeat imaging one month later revealed new gadolinium-enhancing lesions, correlating with the patient's clinical relapse. Alternative causes of disease progression, including radiation-induced demyelination, radionecrosis, opportunistic infections, progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (PML), and development of anti-natalizumab antibodies, were explored and considered less likely. The patient was switched to ofatumumab with subsequent clinical and radiological stability. Given extensive new inflammatory lesions far from the GKRS site, it seems unlikely that the sole mechanism was radiation-induced neurotoxicity. We hypothesize that late delayed radiation side effects caused by GKRS may have enabled peripheral lymphocytes to enter the CNS, counteracting the effects of natalizumab on blocking lymphocyte trafficking through the BBB and possibly contributing to MS relapse.

papers.abstract: The optimal salvage therapy for relapsed germ cell tumors (GCTs) remains undefined and the optimal timing for high-dose chemotherapy (HD-CT) is unclear. We analyzed data from the European Society for Blood and Marrow Transplantation registry to evaluate contemporary outcomes in patients treated with HD-CT across salvage lines. We extracted data of adult males with GCTs (excluding mediastinal primary) who received one or more courses of HD-CT with carboplatin and etoposide between 2000 and 2022. Patients treated within 3 months from diagnosis were excluded, as this was considered upfront therapy. Time from diagnosis to first HD-CT (TT) was categorized in 3-6, 6-12, and >12 months. A Cox model with restricted cubic splines was used to evaluate the nonlinear effect of TT on survival. Data from a total of 2204 patients were analyzed. Histology was available for 1074, of whom 69% had nonseminoma. Among 969 patients with primary site information, 69% had testicular GCT. International Prognostic Factors Study Group (IPFSG) categories were available for 500 patients: 17% very high, 38% high, 31% intermediate, 10% low, and 3.6% very low risk. TT was 3-6 months for 280 (13%), 6-12 months for 831 (38%), and >12 months for 1093 (50%). Of the patients, 1118 (51%) received three cycles of HD-CT. Median overall survival (OS) and progression-free survival (PFS) were 36.4 [95% confidence interval (CI) 30.3-58.7] and 9.9 months (95% CI 8.5-12.4), respectively. Spline analysis showed increasing hazard of progression and death with longer TT. No interaction was observed between TT and IPFSG risk for PFS (P = 0.62), whereas a significant interaction was found for OS (P = 0.04) in non-high-risk patients. In the largest contemporary series of salvage HD-carboplatin-etoposide in GCTs, HD-CT was effective regardless of TT as a surrogate of salvage line, with a significant interaction in non-high-risk patients, suggesting a nonlinear association between HD-CT timing and OS.

papers.abstract: The European Society for Medical Oncology (ESMO) Clinical Practice Guidelines for the diagnosis, treatment and follow-up of patients with renal cell carcinoma (RCC) were published in May 2024 and adapted in December 2025 according to previously established standard methodology to produce the Pan-Asian adapted ESMO consensus guidelines for the management of Asian patients with RCC. The adapted guidelines presented in this manuscript represent the consensus opinions reached by a panel of Asian experts in the treatment of patients with RCC representing the oncological societies of China [Chinese Society of Clinical Oncology (CSCO)], Indonesia [Indonesian Society of Hematology and Medical Oncology (ISHMO)], India [Indian Society of Medical and Paediatric Oncology (ISMPO)], Japan [Japanese Society of Medical Oncology (JSMO)], Korea [Korean Society of Medical Oncology (KSMO)], Malaysia [Malaysian Oncological Society (MOS)], The Philippines [Philippine Society of Medical Oncology (PSMO)], Singapore [Singapore Society of Oncology (SSO)], Taiwan [Taiwan Oncology Society (TOS)] and Thailand [Thai Society of Clinical Oncology (TSMO)], coordinated by ESMO and the SSO. The voting was based on scientific evidence and was independent of the current treatment practices, drug access restrictions and reimbursement decisions in the different regions of Asia. The latter are discussed separately in the manuscript. The aim is to provide guidance for the optimisation and harmonisation of the management of patients with RCC across the different countries of Asia, drawing on the evidence provided by both Western and Asian trials. Attention is drawn to the disparity in drug approvals and reimbursement strategies between the different regions.

papers.abstract: Pre-existing psychiatric disorders have been associated with the severity of acute respiratory infections, including COVID-19, particularly in hospitalized populations. However, the underlying mechanisms, especially in community-based populations, remain unknown, limiting preparedness for future pandemics. We investigated the role of genetic liability for psychiatric disorders and related traits in COVID-19 and other respiratory infection severity among individuals reporting SARS-CoV-2 testing and available respiratory symptom data. We included population-based cohort data from Denmark, Estonia, Iceland, Norway, and the United Kingdom (N = 78,507; 62% female; 41% SARS-CoV-2-positive; May 2020-March 2023). Respiratory infection severity was defined by self-reported days bedridden and an eleven-symptom composite score during the acute illness phase. Polygenic scores (PGSs) for eight psychiatric disorders and the personality trait neuroticism indexed genetic liability. Meta-analysed estimates from stepwise-adjusted regression analyses controlling for education, lifestyle, and psychiatric and somatic diagnosis history were used to assess associations between PGSs and acute respiratory infection severity, stratified by COVID-19 status. Higher genetic liability to insomnia, major depression (MD), and neuroticism was consistently associated with longer time bedridden (relative risk ratios per 1 SD change in PGS: 1.07-1.14, 95% confidence intervals [CIs]: 1.03-1.21) and more symptoms (incident rate ratios [IRRs]: 1.02-1.04, 95% CIs: 1.01-1.05) due to COVID-19. PGSs for insomnia, MD, neuroticism, anxiety disorder, bipolar disorder, and schizophrenia were also linked to higher non-COVID-19 symptom count (IRRs: 1.01-1.05, 95% CIs: 1.00-1.07). These associations remained robust after adjustment for lifestyle, education and medical comorbidities. Individuals in the highest MD PGS decile reported 20% more symptoms in non-COVID-19 illness and 10% more in COVID-19 compared with the bottom decile. No consistent associations were detected with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder, alcohol dependence and post-traumatic stress disorder. No genetic link was observed with ischaemic heart disease or type 2 diabetes. Shared genetics may contribute to the link between psychiatric conditions and respiratory infection severity in community settings. Our results underscore the role of psychiatric genetic liability, beyond diagnosed psychiatric disorders, in contributing to both COVID-19 and other respiratory infection severity. These findings provide insights that may improve future risk stratification and public health strategies targeting respiratory viruses.

papers.abstract: The evolution of Earth's mantle redox state is central to understanding the rise of atmospheric oxygen and the development of a habitable planet. However, whether the deep mantle has become increasingly oxidized over geological time and its underlying mechanisms remain debated. Here, we analyze chromium isotopes in 66 ancient volcanic rocks (komatiites and picrites) spanning from 3.48 to 1.87 billion years ago combined with an oxygen fugacity (fO2) estimate (Fe3+/ΣFe) derived from thermodynamic simulations. We find that older Archean samples possess distinct isotopic signatures compared to younger Paleoproterozoic ones. Our modeling indicates that Archean magmas formed under more reducing conditions, driven by less recycled surface material in the deep Earth. These results provide evidence for an oxidation of the mantle from Archean to Paleoproterozoic. Our results link deep geodynamic transitions to the surface Great Oxidation Event through the progressive evolution of the mantle redox state.

papers.abstract: Gap junctions facilitate electrical and metabolic coupling essential for tissue function. Under ischemic conditions (e.g., heart attack or stroke), elevated intracellular calcium (Ca²+) uncouples these communication pathways to limit the spread of cytotoxic signals, yet the structural basis of this protective response remains unclear. Here, using single-particle cryo-EM, we define the Ca²+-dependent gating mechanism of native connexin-46/50 (Cx46/50) gap junction channels. Ca2+ binding promotes an ensemble of N-terminal (NT) domain conformations spanning destabilized and fully gated states. These conformational changes are coupled to coordinated subunit rearrangements that asymmetrically collapse the pore and enable steric occlusion by the NT domains. Comparison with recently resolved low-pH gating structures reveals that distinct physiological stimuli converge on a common NT-centered gating mechanism involving coupled NT displacement and TM2 hinge motion. Long-timescale molecular dynamics simulations identify multiple Ca2+ interaction sites along the permeation pathway and suggest that transient inter-subunit Ca2+ coordination can promote NT destabilization and displacement. Together, these findings support a model in which distributed Ca2+ interactions reshape the energetic landscape of the channel to favor NT-mediated pore closure, unifying previous models of gap junction regulation and providing a mechanistic basis for Ca2+-dependent uncoupling during cellular stress.

papers.abstract: Meningococcal serogroup B (MenB) vaccines containing outer membrane vesicles (OMVs) may provide cross-protection against Neisseria gonorrhoeae infections but vaccine-induced mucosal immune responses remain poorly characterized. This phase 2, double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled trial evaluates the immunogenicity of four-component MenB vaccine (4CMenB) against OMVs from gonococcal strains 1291 and CNG20. Study outcomes were IgG antibody responses (assessed using ELISA) in rectal mucosal secretions (primary), serum (secondary), vaginal secretions and saliva (exploratory). Healthy adults aged 18-49 years, with no history of gonorrhea and low-risk for infection, were randomized 4:1 to receive 4CMenB (N = 41) or placebo (N = 11) on Days 1 and 29, with follow-up to Day 181. At baseline, serum IgG against both gonococcal OMVs is detectable in all participants, and mucosal IgG is present in many. 4CMenB elicits robust serum IgG responses to gonococcal OMVs, peaking at Day 43 and remaining elevated at Day 181. Mucosal responses are low-magnitude and exhibit different kinetics by site, with the highest responses in vaginal secretions, which peak at Day 43, followed by rectal secretions and saliva, which peak at Day 57. Responses are largely absent in placebo recipients. Two-dose 4CMenB induces systemic and mucosal IgG to N. gonorrhoeae, supporting its potential role in gonorrhea prevention. The trial registration number is NCT04722003.

papers.abstract: In early T cell development, thymocytes undergoing positive selection receive relatively weak T cell receptor (TCR) signals. However, the mechanisms by which thymocytes translate weak and transient TCR signals into lineage-defining transcriptional programs remain unclear. Here, we show that SATB1 plays a key role in enhancer activation during positive selection, as it promotes the expression of positive selection-associated genes by enhancing super-enhancer (SE) activation. Notably, SATB1 deficiency disrupts SE topological organization, weakens promoter-enhancer interactions, blunts TCR-induced Ca2+ signaling, and impairs the activation of positive selection genes such as Cd2 and Cd5, leading to defective CD4/CD8 lineage differentiation and abnormal premature thymocyte egress. Furthermore, SATB1 forms liquid-like nuclear condensates that act as scaffolds to build super-enhancer structures, stabilizing enhancer accessibility and enhancing enhancer-promoter interactions. Altogether, our findings suggest that SATB1 plays a crucial role in promoting positive selection by driving super-enhancer reprogramming and establishing enhancer-promotor interactions.

papers.abstract: Precise gene dosage control is critical for cellular identity and development, particularly for imprinted genes, where dosage imbalances are linked to neurodevelopmental disorders. The Mest/Copg2 imprinted locus exemplifies this fine-tuned regulation: while Mest is constitutively paternally expressed, Copg2 shifts from biallelic to maternally-biased expression specifically during neural differentiation, a transition proposed to involve transcriptional interference by the long Mest isoform, MestXL, which extends into Copg2. However, the mechanisms underlying this switch and whether factors beyond MestXL contribute remain unresolved. Using a stem cell-based brain organoid model integrating multi-omic analyses, 3D chromatin mapping, and functional approaches, we challenge the prevailing model by showing that the maternal bias of Copg2 is not solely driven by MestXL-mediated interference. Instead, our data reveal a temporal, stage-specific two-step mechanism: putative enhancer-driven activation of the maternal allele in neural progenitors, followed by MestXL-dependent repression of the paternal allele in neuron-enriched stages. This uncovers an unexpected complexity in imprinted gene dosage regulation during brain development.

papers.abstract: Transcytosis-mediated delivery effectively enhances tumor penetration of nanodrugs but is less efficacious in stroma-rich tumors. Cancer associated fibroblasts (CAF) can represent a physical barrier for drug delivery in tumor cells. Herein, by selectively targeting NPC1L1-cancer associated fibroblasts, surface-displayed cholesterol enhances the delivery of a platinum nanodrug (PtD-Chol) in stroma-rich tumors, restoring anti-tumor efficacy. The findings reveal that PtD-Chol, acting through the 'shared entry portal' of NPC1L1 triggers cross-multicellular transport (CMCT) within tumors, shuttling PtD-Chol across the CAF barrier via the endocytic recycling compartment-endoplasmic reticulum-Golgi pathway, thereby enabling deep penetration into tumor. This strategy restores nanodrug efficacy in CAF-rich refractory tumor models in female mice, and suppresses both primary growth and CAF-driven metastasis via tumor microenvironment remodeling. This proposed nanodrug delivery paradigm offers an approach to tackle the critical barriers of tumor penetration and therapeutic efficacy in nanomedicine.

papers.abstract: Electrochemical dehalogenative deuteration in D2O offers a sustainable and site-specific strategy for synthesizing deuterated molecules. However, this process is limited by restricted deuterium transfer in the interfacial hydrogen bond gap zone at the alkaline interface, resulting in a sluggish reaction rate. Here, an iodide-derived copper catalyst is designed to convert 2-monochloroacetic acid (MCAA) to acetic acid (AA), achieving a yield rate of 1.43 mmol h-1 and lowering the potential by 200 mV compared with that of copper. Mechanistic studies reveal that, as hydrogen bond acceptors, iodide ions enhance the connectivity of interfacial water through I-···H - O - H···O interactions, thereby facilitating deuterium shuttling and resulting in an Eley-Rideal deuteration mechanism. Moreover, the facilitated electron transfer and enhanced adsorption of MCAA induced by chemically adsorbed iodide ions contribute to the activation of MCAA. 19.8 g of AA-d4 is obtained at 2.5 A within 40 h, highlighting the great promise of the iodide-modified strategy in catalyst and microenvironment design.

papers.abstract: Hadal trenches, plunging beyond six kilometers depth, harbor a dynamic yet enigmatic microbial biosphere. From ~10 km depth Kermadec Trench sediments, we integrated metagenomics, in situ metatranscriptomics, and phylogenetics to reconstruct 300 prokaryotic species and 186,496 viral populations. In hadal sediment metagenomes analyzed here, we detect distant horizontal gene transfer (DHGT) across phyla/domains and estimate that it contributes on average ~13% of each genome and accounting for >46.7% of multi-copy gene expansions, with four phyla acquiring more than 30% of their genes via DHGT. These DHGT genes encode critical adaptations, including reactive oxygen species detoxification, aromatic compound degradation, and fatty acid/heme biosynthesis, which help microbes survive extreme pressure, low temperatures, and oligotrophy. While classical mechanisms such as conjugation (~0.27%), transduction (~2.1%), and transformation account for a fraction of events, additional potential gene flow conduits are proposed: magnetotaxis-mediated encounters by magnetotactic bacteria (~17.4% of DHGT events), possibly increasing opportunities for gene exchange. These findings suggest that DHGT can contribute substantially to metabolic diversification in the hadal genomes, representing an evolutionary mode distinct from gradualist Darwinian inheritance and consistent with the idea that episodic acquisition of functional modules can contribute to rapid metabolic diversification.

papers.abstract: Maternal and paternal homologous chromosomes recognize each other and pair during meiosis to ensure accurate chromosome segregation. However, the mechanisms that drive chromosome pairing and their regulation remain poorly understood. To investigate this, we develop a fluorescence reporter-operator system based on the lac operator-lac repressor system, enabling real-time observation of specific genomic loci in live mouse seminiferous tubule tissues. Using 3D time-lapse imaging, we visualize and quantify telomere-led rapid chromosome movements and homologous chromosome pairing. Our results reveal that homologous chromosomes achieve pairing in discrete, well-defined steps. Initially, at the onset of meiosis, chromosomes come together from widely separated positions at an average distance of 4.8 µm, followed by an intermediate stage of pairing at an average distance of 1.7 µm. Finally, close pairing is achieved at an average distance of 0.7 µm, which correlates with the establishment of the synaptonemal complex along the homologs. Further analysis of inter-spot distance dynamics reveals a relatively rapid transition from an initial, widely separated distance to an intermediate stage of chromosome pairing. Complementary studies of recombination mutants using 3D DNA fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) on whole-mounted tubules and immunofluorescence on chromosome spreads reveal that double-strand breaks and early recombination events trigger the transition from a widely separated to an intermediate inter-homolog distance. Subsequently, close pairing requires crossover maturation intermediates and SYCP1/synaptonemal complex. Together, our findings reveal a recurring mechanism of meiotic chromosome pairing and how it is regulated by critical meiotic processes in higher eukaryotes.

papers.abstract: Primary biliary cholangitis (PBC) is a chronic cholestatic liver disease associated with progressive fibrosis, cirrhosis, liver transplantation, and premature mortality. Despite effective therapies, important challenges remain in the diagnosis and management of PBC, including identification of antimitochondrial antibody-negative disease, assessment of response to ursodeoxycholic acid (UDCA), risk stratification, treatment of patients with inadequate response, management of cholestatic pruritus, and prevention of recurrent disease after liver transplantation. The aim of this guideline was to develop evidence-based recommendations addressing these key areas of clinical care. The American Gastroenterological Association (AGA) and the American Association for the Study of Liver Diseases (AASLD) convened a multidisciplinary panel to develop clinical practice recommendations for adults with PBC. Systematic reviews were performed for 6 prioritized clinical questions. The Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluation framework was used to prioritize clinical outcomes and assess evidence, and its Evidence to Decision Framework was used to develop recommendations. The guideline panel agreed on 6 recommendations. These recommendations address the use of PBC-specific antinuclear antibodies in antimitochondrial antibody-negative suspected PBC, UDCA as first-line therapy, liver stiffness measurement for prognostication, peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor agonists for patients with inadequate response or intolerance to UDCA, linerixibat for moderate to severe pruritus, and UDCA prophylaxis post-transplantation to reduce disease recurrence. The certainty of evidence ranged from moderate to very low. The guideline emphasizes early diagnosis, optimization of first-line therapy, risk-based treatment escalation, symptom management, and prevention of post-transplantation disease recurrence to improve patient outcomes and quality of life.

papers.abstract: Colorectal cancer remains a major global health burden, and although population-based screening is beneficial, current programs have notable limitations. Risk-stratified screening has been proposed, yet existing prediction models vary in performance and in the inclusion of predictors. Data-adaptive modeling (machine learning) may strengthen risk prediction but depends on high-quality input data. Expert consensus methods offer a structured way to identify clinically meaningful variables for future tools. To establish expert consensus on the selection of relevant variables and refinement of self-reported questionnaire items for next-generation colorectal cancer risk-prediction tools. A modified Delphi study was conducted with seventeen internationally recognized experts. The process consisted of anonymized, email-based rounds aimed at refining a questionnaire for colorectal cancer risk prediction. Across three iterative rounds, experts rated item relevance, proposed revisions, and identified missing domains while reviewing group-level summaries of ratings and comments. Items not meeting predefined thresholds were removed, and validated lifestyle-related items were incorporated. Consensus was defined as 15 of 17 experts rating an item within a similar three-point range. All seventeen experts completed all rounds. The final I-CRC-RISK Questionnaire comprises 23 items across seven categories: Demography, Health Status, Family Health History, Dietary Patterns, Physical Activity, Smoking, and Alcohol Consumption. Expert consensus was reached for 19 items. The I-CRC-RISK Questionnaire provides an expert-informed set of self-reported variables to support future risk prediction efforts. It offers a structured basis for further validation and psychometric testing before prospective data collection may be undertaken. This foundational work could enhance the predictive performance of both traditional and machine-learning approaches by improving the consistency and relevance of input data.

papers.abstract: Existing deep learning models for predicting biochemical recurrence (BCR) after radical prostatectomy often ignore the biological context beyond the tumor. This study aims to develop and validate a transformer-based model combining multi-regional magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) features and clinical data to improve BCR prediction after radical prostatectomy in prostate cancer (PCa). We enrolled 232 Pca patients from three medical centers between 2013 and 2020. Multi-parametric MRI sequences, including T2-weighted fat-suppressed and diffusion-weighted imaging, were collected before surgery. Patients from centers 1 and 2 were assigned to a discovery cohort (training: n = 146; internal validation: n = 36), and patients from center 3 (n = 50) formed an external test cohort. A transformer-based deep learning (DL) model was developed using imaging features from intratumoral, peritumoral, and periprostatic regions, combined with clinical variables. Model performance was evaluated using the area under the curve (AUC), accuracy, sensitivity, and specificity with 95% confidence intervals (CI), and prognostic value was assessed via Kaplan-Meier (K-M) survival analysis. The combined three-region MRI-based model demonstrated superior predictive performance for BCR risk across all sets, with an AUC of 0.801 (0.663-0.920) on the external test set and an AUC of 0.799 (0.715-0.872) on the validation set. Notably, the integrated DL model, which combined MRI data with clinical characteristics, outperformed the MRI-based and clinical models. The three-region with clinical combined model improved AUCs from 0.801 (95% CI: 0.663-0.920) to 0.863 (95% CI: 0.697-0.975) on the external test set and from 0.799 (95% CI: 0.715-0.872) to 0.832 (95% CI: 0.746-0.904) on the validation set. K-M curve analysis revealed that the integrated model provided significantly better predictions than the MRI-based and clinical models (p < 0.0001). By combining intratumoral, peritumoral, and periprostatic regions from multi-parametric MRI with clinical data, the transformer-based DL model provides a multimodal approach for predicting BCR in PCa patients.

papers.abstract: Non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) is among the leading causes of cancer-related deaths worldwide. Previous treatment regimens often have limited efficacy due to drug resistance and recurrence. Metabolic reprogramming participates in the initiation and progression of NSCLC, with prominent changes in lipid metabolism. Mutations in specific driver genes directly remodel lipid metabolic reprogramming in NSCLC by rewiring lipid synthesis, uptake, and catabolism, which confers cancer cells with enhanced proliferative and metastatic capacity. On this basis, targeted lipid metabolism reprogramming has become a promising new direction for the treatment of NSCLC. In this review, we examined the alterations in lipid metabolism in NSCLC, explored the mechanisms by which driver gene mutations change lipid metabolism in NSCLC, and provided possible therapeutic strategies targeting key lipid metabolism pathways at the current stage, aiming to offer a theoretical basis and prospects for the development of novel therapies targeting specific gene mutation subtypes of NSCLC.

papers.abstract: Over the past 5 decades, small cell lung cancer (SCLC) has persisted as one of the most formidable malignancies, largely attributed to its aggressive early metastasis, limited therapeutic arsenal in both first-line and subsequent treatments, and rapid onset of treatment resistance. The dawn of a new era in the treatment of SCLC appeared in 2018, with the introduction of first-line chemotherapy combined with immune checkpoint inhibitors, as well as tarlatamab for later-line treatment. However, the improvements in survival, although tangible, were still unsatisfactory. Therefore, this review focuses on unraveling the mechanisms underlying cancer initiation, progression, and particularly metastasis, as well as emerging advances in molecular subtyping and drug resistance from the epigenetic perspective. Simultaneously, we outline their hallmark characteristics—high plasticity, heterogeneity, redundancy, and ambiguity driven by intercellular crosstalk under spatiotemporal dependency. Furthermore, we highlight the evolving progress of various successful drugs or therapeutic strategies and molecular biomarkers in clinical practice for SCLC, as well as promising agents under investigation. Finally, we also discuss how to leverage artificial intelligence and innovative biomedical technologies, as well as learn from various challenges in order to improve the therapeutic landscape of SCLC.

papers.abstract: Abstract Poly (ADP-ribose) polymerase inhibitors (PARPi) exploit synthetic lethality to treat BRCA1/2-mutated ovarian cancer, yet clinical responses are often incomplete and resistance frequently emerges. PARPi exert cytotoxic effects by inhibiting single-strand break repair and trapping PARP on DNA, which impedes replication fork progression and generates lethal double-strand breaks. However, tumor cells can mitigate these effects through the activation of alternative DNA repair mechanisms. In this study, we investigated the role of translesion DNA synthesis (TLS), a DNA damage tolerance pathway in which specialized polymerases bypass DNA lesions to sustain replication, in mediating PARPi resistance using homologous recombination (HR)–deficient epithelial ovarian cancer cell lines, patient-derived organoids (PDO), and orthotopic xenograft models. PARPi treatment markedly slowed replication fork progression and activated TLS. Genetic depletion of the TLS scaffold protein REV1 and TLS polymerase η (Polη, encoded by POLH) exacerbated olaparib-induced replication stress, impaired fork restart, and sensitized BRCA1/2-deficient cells to PARPi. Importantly, pharmacologic TLS inhibition with JH-RE-06 synergized with olaparib to enhance cytotoxicity in HR-deficient cells and PDOs, whereas in vivo combination therapy delayed or prevented resistance and achieved sustained tumor regression. Notably, TLS blockade also suppressed the emergence of BRCA2 reversion mutations in BRCA2-mutated ovarian cancer cells and prevented the development of olaparib resistance during chronic olaparib exposure. Collectively, these findings demonstrate that TLS, particularly Polη-dependent bypass, is a critical mechanism enabling replication fork rescue and survival under PARPi therapy. Targeting TLS provides a promising therapeutic strategy to augment PARPi efficacy and prevent resistance in BRCA-deficient ovarian cancer. Significance: Translesion synthesis drives PARP inhibitor resistance by rescuing stalled replication forks and promoting BRCA reversion, which can be overcome by targeting Polη to enhance therapeutic sensitivity and durability in BRCA-deficient ovarian cancer.

papers.abstract: Abstract Objectives Copper is an essential redox cofactor required for mitochondrial respiration and antioxidant defense, yet its dysregulation creates a therapeutic vulnerability that can be exploited by copper active agents. Elesclomol and neocuproine are two potent copper active compounds, but whether they induce the same form of cuproptosis , a copper-dependent cell death mechanism, has remained unclear. We aimed to elucidate the cytotoxic programs triggered by these two agents and to determine whether distinct mechanistic forms of cuproptosis exist. Methods Our study integrates limited-proteolysis proteomics to identify compound-responsive changes in protein structural accessibility, whole-genome CRISPRa (activation) screening, transcriptomic analysis of 436 CCLE cancer cell lines, mass spectrometry-based analysis of cellular and tumor copper abundance, genetic perturbation studies, mitochondrial functional assays, and mitophagy analyses. Pathway enrichment and functional validation were used to identify adaptive survival programs and compound-specific copper-handling mechanisms. Results Building on the previously established FDX1-dependent cuproptosis mechanism induced by elesclomol, we designate this pathway as canonical cuproptosis (c-CPX) and identify neocuproine as inducing a mechanistically distinct, FDX1-independent form of cuproptosis, which we term non-canonical cuproptosis (nc-CPX). In c-CPX, FDX1 mediates elesclomol delivered Cu(II) to Cu(I) reduction, leading to rapid oligomerization of lipoylated mitochondrial proteins and subsequent proteotoxic stress. In contrast, neocuproine induces n-CPX, a FDX1-independent copper-dependent death program that preferentially engages neocuproine stabilized Cu(I)-handling and stress-adaptation networks. Despite its FDX1 independence, neocuproine rapidly induces oligomerization of lipoylated DLAT, identifying an early point of convergence with canonical cuproptosis. Large-scale analysis of CCLE cancer cell lines further revealed that sensitivity to both neocuproine and elesclomol is associated with enrichment of oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS) transcriptional programs. Notably, neocuproine-sensitive cancer cells additionally displayed significantly higher mesenchymal/EMT scores across multiple independent gene-expression signatures, linking an OXPHOS-enriched, mesenchymal cell state to increased susceptibility to neocuproine-induced copper-dependent cell death. Limited-proteolysis profiling identified ATOX1 among the prominent neocuproine-responsive proteins. Functional validation demonstrated that ATOX1 depletion partially attenuates neocuproine-induced cytotoxicity, but not elesclomol toxicity, while ATOX1 loss itself promotes DLAT oligomerization, supporting a specific contribution of ATOX1-dependent Cu(I) handling to nc-CPX. CRISPRa screening further revealed that adaptive programs enriched during neocuproine exposure predominantly involve proteasomal and lysosomal pathways; whereas elesclomol is associated with distinct signaling and bioenergetic programs, including PI3K, JAK–STAT, and MAPK pathways, as well as oxidative phosphorylation and glutathione metabolism. The functional relevance of the neocuproine-associated pathways was supported by enhanced cytotoxicity upon pharmacological inhibition of proteasomal or lysosomal function. Despite their divergent initiation mechanisms, both canonical and non-canonical cuproptosis converge on early oligomerization of lipoylated mitochondrial proteins followed by Fe–S-protein loss, respiratory-chain dysfunction, mitochondrial remodeling, impaired mitochondrial quality control, and respiratory failure. Both compounds also induce cytoplasmic and mitochondrial ROS and late apoptotic features. Continuous N-acetylcysteine (NAC) exposure reduced the labile intracellular Cu(I) signal and rescued cytotoxicity; whereas NAC pretreatment followed by washout did not protect against subsequent neocuproine or elesclomol exposure. Together with the lack of rescue by caspase inhibition and the delayed appearance of apoptotic features, these findings support ROS accumulation and apoptosis as predominantly downstream consequences rather than defining initiating mechanisms. Conclusion Our findings establish a mechanistic framework distinguishing canonical FDX1 dependent cuproptosis from non-canonical FDX1 independent cuproptosis. Rather than representing separate downstream death programs, c-CPX and nc-CPX constitute distinct upstream copper-handling routes that converge on a shared mitochondria-centered proteotoxic program. These results provide insight into copper-driven cytotoxicity and suggest FDX1 dependency, ATOX1-dependent copper-handling, EMT/OXPHOS state, and proteostasis pathways as candidate biomarkers and therapeutic vulnerabilities for further investigation.

papers.abstract: Abstract Background Genetic mosaicism is a well-recognized consequence of CRISPR–Cas9 genome editing, yet its characterization remains challenging, especially when it involves low-frequency structural variants. A comprehensive analysis of mosaicism requires deep and unbiased sequencing of the target loci, with accurate single-molecule reads. Methods We performed amplification-free PureTarget PacBio sequencing to investigate CRISPR-Cas9 outcomes at on-target and off-target sites in genome edited zebrafish and their offspring. CRISPR-Cas9 genome editing was performed by micro-injection in fertilized eggs at the single-cell stage. Results Thirty samples from pooled larvae and individual zebrafish were successfully sequenced, resulting in > 1100x average target coverage. The PacBio reads reached an exceptional accuracy (QV39) over the target regions, with every read originating from a unique DNA molecule. The two haplotypes of the target loci displayed a balanced depth of coverage, while long-range PCR of the same samples resulted in skewed data. Further analysis of the PureTarget data revealed widespread genetic mosaicism in individual founder (F0) fish, with up to 18 distinct on-target events and 11 off-target events present in a single adult founder. Several CRISPR-Cas9 editing outcomes, including large structural variants and off-target mutations, were inherited to the F1 generation. Notably, as many as seven unique editing events were found among sibling F1 juvenile offspring derived from a single founder pair, thereby confirming the presence of genetic mosaicism in germ cells of founder zebrafish. This implies that some consequences of CRISPR-Cas9 editing may emerge only in the second generation. We also analyzed DNA methylation signals in the PureTarget data but did not observe altered 5mC CpG levels in genome edited samples. Conclusions PureTarget enables efficient, accurate, and unbiased profiling of genetic mosaicism and DNA methylation at pre-defined genomic regions. Our results show that CRISPR–Cas9–induced mosaicism is widespread and represents an important factor to consider in genome editing experiments.

papers.abstract: Abstract Background Prolonged fasting may improve metabolic health, but controlled data in healthy adults with longer follow-up and multi-omics profiling are limited. We investigated the immediate and 12-week follow-up effects of a 5-day fasting intervention on body composition, gut microbiome, and circulating and fecal metabolites, and assessed whether baseline characteristics predict individual weight-loss response. Methods In a randomized, waitlist-controlled trial, 38 healthy adults completed a 5-day fasting intervention with 12-week follow-up (LEANER study). Outcomes included body mass index and body composition, gut microbiome composition, and plasma and fecal metabolites. Changes over time and between groups were evaluated using regression-based models and paired non-parametric tests, as appropriate. Additionally, permutation-based multivariate testing was performed on microbiome and metabolome data. Twelve-week body weight response was predicted using data-driven machine learning with cross-validation, followed by external validation in three independent cohorts undergoing prolonged fasting protocols. Results Fasting reduced body mass index acutely, predominantly driven by loss of fat mass, and these improvements partially persisted at 12 weeks. Fasting induced marked shifts in gut microbiome composition and in plasma and fecal metabolites. Post-fasting and longer-term changes in microbial diversity were associated with baseline microbiome diversity. A model combining baseline microbiome and clinical variables predicted body mass index response at 12 weeks; prominent predictors included an unclassified Faecalibacterium species, Oscillibacter sp. 50_27, low-density lipoprotein cholesterol, and systolic blood pressure. The model generalized to three independent cohorts, including individuals with metabolic syndrome, patients with multiple sclerosis exposed to repeated fasting, and healthy volunteers fasting for 6–12 days. Conclusions In healthy adults, a 5-day prolonged fasting intervention produces robust short-term metabolic changes with partial persistence and consistent remodeling of the gut microbiome and metabolite profiles. Baseline microbiome and clinical characteristics can help stratify expected longer-term responses, supporting the development of individualized fasting-based interventions. papers.abstract: Epstein-Barr virus (EBV)-associated gastric cancer (EBVaGC) is a molecularly distinct, highly immunogenic gastric cancer subtype, yet the role of tertiary lymphoid structure (TLS) during therapy remains unclear. Using a large locally advanced EBVaGC cohort (144 samples), combined with spatial transcriptomics (11 samples) and a single-cell atlas (77 samples), we show that EBVaGC exhibits enhanced TLS formation compared with EBV-negative gastric cancer, with invasive-margin TLS (IM-TLS) predicting favorable prognosis. Neoadjuvant chemotherapy disrupts TLS formation and shows limited efficacy in EBVaGC. Recurrent tumors display increased neutrophil infiltration around TLS, with aging neutrophils recruited via the CXCR4-CXCL12 axis. Mechanistically, chemotherapy induces EBV reactivation, activating neutrophil pattern recognition receptors and promoting neutrophil extracellular trap (NET) formation, which impairs lymphocyte migration and TLS maturation. These findings identify EBV reactivation-driven neutrophil aging and NET formation as a mechanism underlying poor prognosis in EBVaGC, positioning IM-TLS as a prognostic biomarker and neutrophil dysfunction as a therapeutic target.

papers.abstract: Mass spectrometry (MS)-based single-cell proteomics (SCP) enables proteome-wide analysis at single-cell resolution, offering insights into cellular heterogeneity, biological processes, and disease mechanisms. However, conventional nanoLC-MS workflows are constrained by long gradients and low throughput, limiting their application to small cohorts. Here, we present a multicolumn nanoLC-MS platform that achieves 5-minute separation windows with 100% duty cycles at ~100 nL/min, enabling the analysis of up to 288 single cells per day. The system provides stable peptide separation, negligible carryover, and robust retention-time reproducibility across nearly 1200 consecutive injections. We successfully analyze more than 4000 samples at nearly 288 samples per day (SPD) throughput. The platform identifies ~5000 proteins per 250 pg digest injection and an average of ~4000 proteins per single HeLa cell with maxima exceeding 5100, which is comparable to state-of-the-art longer-gradient workflows. Quantitative benchmarking with mixed-species standards confirm the quantitative accuracy is largely maintained during extended acquisition. Applying the workflow to 783 LPS-treated RAW264.7 macrophages reveals substantial cellular heterogeneity under a uniform inflammatory stimulus. Together, these results establish a robust and scalable platform for high-throughput SCP, enabling thousands of single-cell analyses within a single study while maintaining deep proteome coverage and biological interpretability.

papers.abstract: Hepatocellular carcinoma and depression frequently co-occur, yet the mechanisms linking them remain unclear. Here, we show that chronic stress, systemic inflammation, or neuropathic pain are associated with hepatocellular carcinoma progression in male mice. Chronic stress hyperactivates a glutamatergic paraventricular hypothalamic nucleus → cholinergic dorsal motor nucleus of the vagus → liver circuit, increasing intratumoral acetylcholine. Single-cell transcriptomics identifies acetylcholine-responsive Chrna9+ epithelial cells that interact with macrophages through COL1A1/2-CD44-STAT3 signaling to promote CXCL1 production. Acetylcholine also promotes tumor cell proliferation through CHRNA9. Circulating CXCL1 crosses the blood-brain barrier and activates hypothalamic glutamatergic neurons, exacerbating depression-like behaviors and establishing a liver-brain feedback loop. Silencing the hypothalamic vagal circuit, tumor-specific Chrna9 knockdown, or systemic CXCL1 neutralization restrains tumor progression and alleviates depression-like behaviors. These findings identify a neural and immune mechanism linking chronic stress to hepatocellular carcinoma progression in male mice.

papers.abstract: Race and ethnicity play an important role in breast cancer disparities; however, these variables are not consistently reported in research articles. Our study evaluates contemporary trends in racial and ethnic demographic reporting in clinical breast surgery research over a six-year period. PubMed search engine was queried for breast surgery related clinical research articles published from January 2017 to June 2023. The four breast journals with the highest impact factors were evaluated: Annals of Surgical Oncology, Breast Cancer Research and Treatment, Clinical Breast Cancer, and The Breast Journal. Statistical analyses were conducted using chi-square, Fisher's exact tests, or Cochran-Armitage Trend Test. Among 288 studies included, 181 (62.9%) reported any race/ethnicity. Studies were divided based on year of publication into three study periods: 2017-2018 (n = 108), 2019-2020 (n = 87), 2021-2023 (n = 93). Studies consistently reported White race across all time periods (100% vs. 96.4% vs. 100.0%) (p = 0.09), along with Black race (79.3% vs. 76.4% vs. 88.2%, p = 0.20), Asian race (50.0% vs. 45.5% vs. 60.3%, p = 0.24), Hispanic ethnicity (46.6% vs. 47.3 vs. 48.5%, p = 0.97), and "Other" race (55.2% vs. 61.8% vs. 66.2%, p = 0.45). Reporting of any race/ethnicity was found to have increased in recent years (53.7% vs. 63.2% vs. 73.1%, p < 0.01), only up to 73.1% in 2021-2023. Race reporting in high-impact breast surgery journals has increased significantly from 2017 to 2023, although only reaching 73.1% in 2021-2023. Specific populations, including Hispanics and Asian-Americans, remain underrepresented. While increasing, race reporting remains limited in clinical breast research, underscoring the need for more consistent and comprehensive research standards.

papers.abstract: Evidence is inconsistent regarding an association between alcohol consumption and survival following a breast cancer diagnosis; therefore, we examined how change in alcohol consumption affects all-cause mortality (ACM) in a population of breast cancer survivors. We prospectively assessed pre-diagnosis, pre- to post-diagnosis, and post-diagnosis change in alcohol consumption among 1,558 postmenopausal women (mean age-at-diagnosis: 71 years) diagnosed with non-metastatic invasive breast cancer from the American Cancer Society Cancer Prevention Study-II Nutrition Cohort (baseline: 1992-1993). Five categories of alcohol intake were determined at each assessment; change in alcohol consumption was categorized as stable, quit, reduced, and increased. Change occurred at a median of two years before (pre-diagnosis) and two years after (post-diagnosis) diagnosis. Cox proportional hazards regression was used to estimate adjusted hazard ratios (HR) and 95% confidence intervals (CI) for the associations between change groups and ACM. Over a median follow-up of 12.6 years, 750 women died (130 breast cancer deaths). Compared to stable consumption, the association between cessation and ACM varied by change interval: pre-diagnosis (HR:0.91, CI:0.69-1.21), pre- to post-diagnosis: (HR:1.39, CI:1.12-1.73), post-diagnosis: (HR:0.98, CI:0.70-1.35). Alcohol reduction was not associated with ACM. Among women consuming ≥ 1 drink/day pre-diagnosis, increasing consumption elevated ACM risk (HR:1.83, 95%CI:1.02-3.31). Alcohol reduction or cessation was not associated with a decrease in ACM among older breast cancer survivors. Among those drinking ≥ 1 drink/day, an increase in consumption pre-diagnosis was associated with higher mortality. Findings may be limited by uncontrolled confounding, a low prevalence of heavy drinking, or an insufficient duration of sustained change.

papers.abstract: Patients with high-grade glioma reach surgery during the initial, index hospitalization (urgent), or through scheduled/outpatient pathways. There is a paucity of literature examining what patients require expedited versus elective surgery. This single-center retrospective study describes complications, utilization, and survival by pathway. Adults with WHO grade 3-4 gliomas undergoing primary resection (2021-2026) were classified as urgent (admitted without a planned resection date) or scheduled (discharged and readmitted for planned surgery, or managed exclusively as an outpatient). Primary outcomes were 30-day complications and days alive at home within 30 days of admission for resection (DAH-30). Secondary outcomes were progression free and overall survival. Survival was analyzed with propensity-score overlap weighting and Cox regression. Of 166 patients, 122 underwent urgent resection and 44 scheduled resections; 40 of 44 (91%) proceeded as planned. Urgent patients more often had midline shift (62% vs. 32%), less often seizure (15% vs. 39%), and lower Karnofsky scores (70 vs. 80); all p ≤ 0.002. They had longer index hospitalizations (median 8 vs. 3 days, p < 0.001) and fewer days at home (median 15 vs. 27; adjusted difference - 8.9 days, 95% CI - 12.9 to - 4.8). Complication rates (36% vs. 30%; adjusted OR 1.15, 95% CI 0.52-2.62) and overall survival (median 15.4 vs. 19.0 months, p = 0.758) did not differ detectably. Scheduled resection identified a distinct population, recognizable at initial evaluation by preserved performance status and the absence of midline shift. These patients spent more days at home and required shorter hospitalizations; no harm signal was observed. These data suggest that a substantial proportion of patients with newly diagnosed presumed high grade gliomas can be managed effectively in an expedited, outpatient basis.

papers.abstract: Our purpose was to compare the safety and toxicity profiles of concurrent versus sequential administration of cyclin-dependent kinase 4/6 inhibitors (CDK4/6i) and postoperative radiotherapy (RT) in patients with Positive regional nodes, operable, hormone receptor-positive (HR+), HER2-negative breast cancer (HER2-). We conducted a real-world, multicenter retrospective cohort study enrolling 364 patients with node-positive, operable HR+/HER2- breast cancer who received postoperative radiotherapy combined with CDK4/6 inhibitors between January 2019 and December 2024. Propensity score matching (PSM) was performed to balance baseline covariates between the two arms, yielding 87 patients in each matched group. The primary endpoint was permanent CDK4/6i discontinuation, and secondary endpoints included dose reduction, drug substitution, grade ≥3 toxicities, and symptomatic radiation-induced lung injury (sRILI). No significant intergroup differences were observed in CDK4/6i discontinuation rates before or after PSM (unmatched: 10.4% vs. 8.4%, P=0.536; PSM-matched: 10.3% vs. 9.2%, P=0.798). Similar non-significant findings were identified for dose reduction and drug substitution across unmatched and matched cohorts. For severe toxicities, univariate analysis of the unmatched cohort revealed a significantly higher rate of grade ≥3 drug eruption in the concurrent arm (4.3% vs. 0.4%, unadjusted P=0.013), while this association attenuated to borderline statistical significance after covariate balancing via PSM (4.6% vs. 0.0%, unadjusted P=0.059). No significant between-group differences were detected in sRILI, interstitial pneumonia, grade ≥3 radiation dermatitis, grade ≥3 diarrhea, or hematologic toxicities pre- and post-matching. All grade ≥3 drug eruptions occurred outside radiation fields and presented as diffuse maculopapular rashes involving the trunk and extremities, consistent with CDK4/6i-related hypersensitivity. Concurrent CDK4/6 inhibitor therapy and postoperative RT demonstrate a manageable safety and tolerance profile. Given that treatment discontinuation due to ≥G 3 toxicities was observed in both groups, close toxicity monitoring and comprehensive management throughout the treatment course should be implemented when combining RT with CDK4/6i.

papers.abstract: Craniospinal irradiation (CSI) is used for leptomeningeal carcinomatosis (LMC), yet comparative data between proton CSI (pCSI) and photon volumetric modulated arc therapy CSI (xCSI) are limited. We evaluated clinical outcomes and longitudinal toxicity profiles following pCSI versus xCSI in patients with solid tumor LMC. We retrospectively identified adults with solid tumor LMC treated with CSI at a single institution from 2020 to 2025. Toxicities were graded per CTCAE v5.0 at baseline, during treatment, and at 1, 3, and 6 months post-CSI. Overall survival (OS) and central nervous system progression-free survival (CNS-PFS) were estimated using Kaplan-Meier methods; Cox models evaluated OS associations. 45 patients initiated CSI (18 xCSI, 27 pCSI). Grade ≥ 3 lymphopenia during treatment was similar (75% xCSI versus 56% pCSI; p = 0.43), whereas Grade ≥ 3 thrombocytopenia occurred only with xCSI (29% versus 0%; p = 0.04). At 3 months, Grade ≥ 3 lymphopenia was higher with pCSI (79% versus 17%; p = 0.02). Non-hematologic Grade ≥ 3 toxicities were rare. OS did not significantly differ (median 8.5 months pCSI versus 4.8 months xCSI; p = 0.50), nor did CNS-PFS (5.9 versus 3.0 months; p = 0.20). On multivariable analysis, worse OS was associated with higher extracranial tumor burden (HR 2.77, 95% CI, 1.20-6.40) and performance status (HR 2.88, 95% CI, 1.01-8.23), but not modality. No statistically significant modality differences in OS or CNS-PFS were detected; baseline performance status and extracranial burden were associated with OS. VMAT-based CSI represents a practical alternative in settings without protons, with careful monitoring of acute hematologic toxicity.

papers.abstract: NF1-associated high-grade gliomas (HGGs) are rare, biologically heterogeneous tumors with poor outcomes. Although MEK inhibitors (MEKis) are established options for selected NF1-associated low-grade gliomas, their role in NF1-associated HGG remains undefined. We describe clinical and radiographic outcomes with MEKis, including mirdametinib. We retrospectively reviewed adult patients with NF1-associated HGG treated at The University of Texas MD Anderson Cancer Center who initiated selumetinib, mirdametinib, or dabrafenib plus trametinib from December 1, 2019, to January 31, 2026. Outcomes included radiographic response and Kaplan-Meier estimates of progression-free survival (PFS) and overall survival (OS) from MEKi initiation. Progression was defined as the earliest documented radiographic or clinical evidence of progression. Nine patients were included. Median age at HGG onset was 34 years (range, 22-58), and median Karnofsky Performance Status at MEKi initiation was 60 (range, 50-90). Diagnoses were high-grade astrocytoma with piloid features (n = 6), IDH-wildtype glioblastoma (n = 2), and IDH-wildtype HGG/not otherwise specified (n = 1). Most patients received MEKi after prior local and/or systemic therapy. Among three patients treated with mirdametinib, two evaluable patients achieved partial response by Response Assessment in Neuro-Oncology criteria. Six patients received selumetinib for 1-7 cycles, and one patient received dabrafenib/trametinib for 2 cycles. Stable disease was the best response among the remaining evaluable patients. Median PFS and OS from MEKi initiation were 2.9 and 9.4 months, respectively. Radiographic partial responses were observed in two patients with NF1-associated HGG treated with mirdametinib, but durability of benefit was limited. The best response with selumetinib and dabrafenib/trametinib was stable disease in evaluable patients. Larger prospective studies are needed to define the role of MEK inhibition in this population.

papers.abstract: Serine metabolism is of growing biologic and therapeutic interest in cancer. Upregulation of the serine synthesis pathway (SSP) can fuel tumor growth, and cancers with this phenotype are often sensitive to. SSP inhibitors. In parallel, dietary restriction of serine and glycine (SG) can suppress some cancers, but the determinants of sensitivity to. this approach are poorly understood. This is especially true in acute myeloid leukemia (AML), where serine metabolism has been less explored. We report that a subset of human AML cell lines and primary samples are completely dependent on external serine, known as serine auxotrophy. These leukemias consistently suppressed the SSP enzyme PSAT1, failed to. synthesize serine, responded to. SG restriction in vivo, and were rescued by restoring PSAT1. We also found that SG restriction synergized with venetoclax in serine auxotrophic AML, and that MECOM rearrangement was strongly associated with PSAT1 suppression and serine auxotrophy. These findings define a metabolically distinct AML subtype and nominate it for targeting by SG restriction.

papers.abstract: Inguinal lymph node dissection (ILND) remains a cornerstone of nodal management in penile cancer, providing definitive treatment for clinically node-positive disease and surgical staging for high-risk clinically node-negative patients when dynamic sentinel node biopsy (DSNB) is unavailable. Despite its oncological importance, ILND is associated with substantial morbidity. Over the past decade, minimally invasive (MI) approaches have emerged as alternatives to open ILND, with the potential to reduce wound-related complications while maintaining oncological efficacy. This Surgery in Motion article provides a practical overview of contemporary open, video-endoscopic (VEIL), and robot-assisted (RAVEIL) ILND techniques, integrating anatomical principles, technical variations, and current clinical evidence. Open ILND remains the reference approach, particularly in patients with advanced nodal disease, while MI techniques may be considered in selected patients with limited nodal disease at experienced centres. Across all approaches, meticulous adherence to anatomical templates, appropriate patient selection, and preservation of lymphatic and vascular structures where oncologically feasible are key principles for minimising morbidity. Emerging robotic and image-guided technologies may further refine ILND, although their clinical benefits and long-term oncological outcomes require further evaluation. This stepwise educational review and accompanying surgical video aim to support surgical training, standardisation, and safe implementation of contemporary ILND techniques.

papers.abstract: Active surveillance (AS) is a recommended option for favorable-risk Gleason grade group 2 (GG2) prostate cancer (PCa), but uptake varies. To describe the nature of progression of confirmed GG2 disease in a well-annotated AS cohort. Participants at the University of California, San Francisco, were diagnosed with cT1-2N0/xM0/x, prostate-specific antigen (PSA) <20 ng/ml, core positivity ≤50%, and GG2 PCa without expansile cribriform or intraductal carcinoma (EC/IDC) at diagnosis, with two or more biopsies on AS from 2000 to 2025. Active surveillance. Outcomes were upgrade (GG3 or higher), volume increase to >50%, EC/IDC, disease progression (upgrade, volume increase, or EC/IDC), active treatment, recurrence (biochemical recurrence or salvage treatment) after radical prostatectomy (RP), metastasis, and PCa-specific mortality (PCSM). Cox proportional hazards regression models were used to identify risk factors for AS outcomes. A total of 329 men were included. At 5 and 10 yr of follow-up, respectively, the upgrade rate was 31% and 58%, volume increase rate was 22% and 31%, EC/IDC development rate was 10% and 41%, disease progression rate was 44% and 79%, active treatment rate was 46% and 65%, and metastasis rate was 0.80% and 3.3%. The 5-yr post-RP recurrence rate was 32%. No PCSM events were recorded within 10 yr. PSA density (PSAD) and positive baseline multiparametric magnetic resonance imaging (mpMRI; Prostate Imaging Reporting and Data System 4-5) were associated with disease progression and active treatment. Limitations include the single-institution cohort, a largely Caucasian population, and incomplete mpMRI and genomic testing. Men with confirmed favorable-risk GG2 PCa on AS have moderate rates of disease progression requiring treatment at 10 yr. Metastasis and PCSM rates were low, but confidence intervals are wide and require external validation. Positive mpMRI and increased PSAD were associated with disease progression and can help tailor AS intensity.

papers.abstract: There are substantial regional differences in prostate cancer (PCa) epidemiology reflecting differences in risk factors, screening, management, and access to care. To assess geographical differences and temporal trends in PCa incidence and mortality and PCa risk factors. Estimated incidence and mortality data for the year 2024 and projections to 2050 based on the assumption that 2024 age-specific incidence and mortality rates remain unchanged (not accounting for changes in risk factors and/or treatments) in 185 countries were derived from the International Agency for Research on Cancer's GLOBOCAN 2024 database. A narrative review of the literature summarized risk factors and preventive measures. Worldwide, 1.55 million new PCa cases were estimated in 2024, with an age-standardized rate (ASR) for incidence of 29 per 100 000. Northern America had the highest all-age incidence ASR (81), and South-Central Asia the lowest (7.2). PCa caused an estimated 420 000 deaths (7.5 per 100 000), with the highest mortality ASRs in the Caribbean (29) and the lowest in South-Central Asia (3.4). By 2050, new cases are projected to be 2.88 million (+86%) and deaths 924 000 (+120%), with the largest relative increases in Africa (+156%). Prostate-specific antigen-based screening influences both incidence and geographic variation. Family history, germ line pathogenic variants, polygenic risk scores, and ancestry are risk factors. Disparities in men of African versus European ancestry reflect both tumor biology and unequal access to care, with mortality gaps narrowing in equal-access health systems. No single nutrient or supplement has been shown to reduce PCa incidence. Cigarette smoking and obesity are associated with PCa-specific mortality, whereas physical activity and plant-based or Mediterranean dietary patterns are associated with a lower risk of disease progression. The global burden of PCa because of population increase and aging is projected to rise substantially by 2050, particularly in low- and middle-income regions. Family history, germ line pathogenic variants, and ancestry are risk factors for PCa. Evidence remains insufficient to support any specific preventive intervention, although smoking, diet, and physical activity may modify risk of progression or mortality.

papers.abstract: Prostate cancer (PCa) is a major malignant tumor threatening men's global health. The plasticizer acetyl tributyl citrate (ATBC), widely used as a substitute for phthalates, is increasingly detected in human tissues; however, its role in PCa cell migration and invasion and the underlying mechanisms remain largely unknown. This study integrated network toxicology, scRNA-seq, transcriptomic analysis, Mendelian randomization (MR), and machine learning. In vitro, LNCaP cell proliferation, migration, and invasion were evaluated after ATBC treatment. ATBC toxicity targets were predicted using public databases. scRNA-seq data were analyzed to identify key cell clusters and candidate genes. Causal relationships between candidate genes and PCa were assessed by MR, and key genes were validated through multiple cohorts and HPA-based immunohistochemistry data. Molecular docking and virtual gene knockout were employed to explore binding affinity and functional impact. In this study, in-vitro experiments were first performed, and it was found that the proliferation, migration and invasion abilities of ATBC-treated LNCaP cells were significantly altered. Subsequently, scRNA-seq data were analyzed to identify key cells (epithelial cells). Next, public databases were used to predict the toxic targets of ATBC, and the results of scRNA-seq and transcriptomic analyses were integrated to screen for potential target genes of ATBC in PCa. Finally, MR and machine-learning techniques were adopted to obtain the key genes (LPCAT1 and PDK1). In addition, molecular docking results for ATBC confirmed favorable binding affinity between the key genes and ATBC. Virtual knockout results also indicated that the key genes played a role in tumor migration and invasion. ATBC exposure may promote PCa migration and invasion by targeting LPCAT1 and PDK1, thereby perturbing cytoskeletal dynamics and metabolic pathways. These findings offer novel mechanistic insights into microplastic-associated PCa progression.

papers.abstract: Tumor-associated macrophages (TAMs) are among the most abundant cells in the tumor microenvironment (TME), with M1 and M2 polarization exhibiting anti-tumorigenic and tumorigenic functions, respectively. Originating from both embryonic precursors and circulating monocytes derived from hematopoietic stem cells, TAMs acquire distinct transcriptional, metabolic, and functional identities shaped by the TME. The interactions in the TME among various cells, including cancerous and non-cancerous cells, can determine the polarization and function of TAMs within the tumor. More recently, TAMs have garnered significant interest as a promising therapeutic target in oncology. The TAMs have been shown to enhance proliferation, metastasis, and angiogenesis in human cancers. Notably, cytokines and chemokines, among others, can regulate the infiltration of TAMs in TME. Given the crucial role of macrophages in regulating inflammation and immune responses, targeting these cells has become a significant focus in cancer immunotherapy. Currently, macrophages have been targeted through three strategies, including suppressing macrophage/monocyte recruitment, depletion of TAMs, and re-education of TAMs. Each of these approaches is being investigated in preclinical models and clinical trials, either as monotherapy or in combination with immune checkpoint inhibitors. TAMs can also be engineered to act as drug delivery tools, carrying nanoparticles directly into tumors. In the clinic, some types of TAMs, marked by proteins like CD163 and CD204, can help predict patient outcomes in several cancers. This review investigates the origins of TAMs and the mechanisms underlying their polarization and metabolism. Furthermore, we study macrophage-driven tumor progression and devising effective targeting strategies, as well as challenges that remain and where the field may go next in macrophage-based cancer treatment. Going forward, combining single-cell profiling with multi-target therapies may offer the best path toward more effective, TAM-based cancer treatments.

papers.abstract: Tobacco smoking is prevalent among patients with rectal cancer, yet its effect on pathologic response to total neoadjuvant therapy (TNT) remains unknown. This study evaluated the association between smoking status and pathologic response to TNT in locally advanced rectal cancer, using the neoadjuvant rectal (NAR) score and pathologic complete response (pCR) rate. This retrospective cohort study used the National Cancer Database to identify adults diagnosed in 2023 with clinical stage Ⅱ-Ⅲ rectal adenocarcinoma who received TNT followed by proctectomy. Smoking status at diagnosis was categorized as never, current, or former. Primary outcomes were favorable NAR score (< 8) and pCR (ypT0N0). Among 1767 patients, 49.7% were never smokers, 30.5% former, and 19.8% current smokers. Rates of favorable NAR score and pCR were highest among never smokers (33.4 and 21.7%), intermediate among former smokers (28.8 and 19.9%), and lowest among current smokers (25.5 and 16.3%). On multivariable analysis, current smoking was associated with lower odds of favorable NAR score than was never smoking (odds ratio 0.59; 95% confidence interval 0.40-0.86). A similar trend was seen for pCR, though this did not reach statistical significance (odds ratio 0.58; 95% confidence interval 0.34-1.00). Former smoking was not significantly different from never smoking in terms of a favorable NAR score or pCR. Current smoking status was independently associated with lower rates of response to TNT in locally advanced rectal cancer, whereas former smoking was not when compared with never smoking. These findings identify active tobacco exposure as a potential modifiable risk factor.

papers.abstract: Mast cells (MCs) display phenotypic heterogeneity across tissues and disease contexts, yet their relevance in melanoma remains unclear. Here, we investigated MC phenotypic programs associated with melanoma progression using high-dimensional phenotyping of MCs co-cultured with melanoma spheroids, trajectory inference, and transcriptomic analyzes. Human melanoma tissues showed differences in MC phenotypic composition despite comparable abundance between outcome groups, with metastatic melanomas enriched for Tryptase⁺ Chymase- MCs. Melanoma exposure induced MC phenotypic remodeling, characterized by loss of lineage- and effector-associated features and increased PD-1 expression, with more pronounced changes following metastatic melanoma co-culture. Trajectory analysis was consistent with a continuum toward a PD-1⁺ Chymase- phenotype, which was detected in melanoma tissues and enriched within intratumoral regions of metastatic melanomas. Experimentally defined protein changes were used to derive two MC-associated transcriptomic signatures with opposing clinical associations, reflecting lineage- and effector-enriched versus melanoma-remodeled programs. The MC-LE signature was associated with favorable survival and interferon-responsive pathways, whereas the MC-MR signature was associated with poorer survival and tumor-associated pathways. These transcriptomic associations extended beyond melanoma across multiple TCGA cancer cohorts, and independent analysis of MCs from healthy skin, basal cell carcinoma, and melanoma showed corresponding differences in MC-LE-related features. Together, these findings support distinct mast cell phenotypic programs associated with melanoma progression and identify a PD-1⁺ Chymase- MC phenotype enriched in metastatic disease and linked to transcriptomic features of poor survival.

papers.abstract: To describe the current landscape of hormone replacement therapy (HRT) to treat surgical menopause following bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy (BSO) in individuals with hereditary ovarian cancer risk in British Columbia, Canada. We aimed to describe current use of HRT, identify factors associated with HRT use and identify potential barriers for uptake and access. Individuals with germline pathogenic/likely pathogenic variants in an ovarian cancer susceptibility gene were identified through the BC Cancer Hereditary Cancer Program (HCP) Progeny database. A cross-sectional survey was administered to collect participant demographics, personal and family cancer history, and participant experiences with HRT. Descriptive statistics were used to characterize the sample and logistic regression used to explore associations between sociodemographic variables and reported HRT use. Open text fields were analyzed using inductive quantitative content analysis. In total, 374 responses were received from 1284 potential participants (29.1% response rate). Of participants who have had a BSO, 41% (101/245) report HRT use. In open-text responses, 22% of participants reported lack of support by healthcare professionals and 26% described gaps in counselling about HRT and surgical menopause. In the regression analysis, HRT use was less likely in individuals who: were of increasing age, reported a history of any cancer type and who reported receiving no counselling about HRT (all p < 0.0011 after Bonferroni correction). Barriers to HRT access and uptake exist for individuals at increased risk of ovarian cancer. Together this data indicates that patients require additional support in this area particularly as it relates to education and resources.

papers.abstract: The antiangiogenic pathway is an effective target for recurrent uterine cervical carcinoma (rCC). This study evaluated the safety and efficacy of cabozantinib monotherapy for rCC. This open-label phase II study (NCT04205799) enrolled patients with rCC who previously received platinum-based chemotherapy. Patients received oral cabozantinib (60 mg daily) until progression or discontinuation from any cause. The main objective was based on joint primary endpoint of efficacy (3-month disease control rate, DCR3) and safety (proportion of patients with grade ≥ 2 (CTCAE v5.0) gastro-intestinal (GI) perforation, GI-vaginal and/or genito-urinary (GU) fistula events) according to a Bryant-and-Day design. Key secondary endpoints were progression-free survival (PFS), duration of response (DOR) and safety. Among 57 patients enrolled, 54 received cabozantinib: median age was 55.5 years, 18 patients (33.3%) had received more than two prior lines of treatment; 28 patients (51.9%) had been previously treated with bevacizumab. Median duration of follow-up was 8.9 months. DCR3 was 46.3% [95% CI, 32.8-60.3]. Fistula/perforation occurred in 5 (9.3%) patients. Objective response rate was 9.3%, with a median DOR of 2.5 months. Median PFS was 2.8 months (95% CI, 2.5-4.6). Grade ≥ 3 treatment-related adverse events occurred in 51.9% of patients, most commonly asthenia (15%), hypertension (9%) and mucositis (6%). Dose reductions and treatment interruptions were reported in 26 (48%) and 24 (44%) patients, respectively. Cabozantinib demonstrates efficacy comparable to other anti-angiogenic monotherapy in rCC; however, modest benefit and toxicity do not support further monotherapy development.

papers.abstract: Abstract Background Timely and comprehensive molecular classification is essential for therapeutic decision-making in pediatric oncology, yet current diagnostic workflows rely on multi-step, time- and resource-intensive testing strategies. We present a standardized whole-genome sequencing approach with adaptive sampling (AS-WGS) using Oxford Nanopore Technologies (ONT) optimized for pediatric cancers, that enables rapid and comprehensive molecular profiling in a single assay. Methods We designed an AS-WGS panel comprising 380 clinically relevant loci that we applied to the sequencing of 36 pediatric cancer and control samples. To support real-time interpretation, we developed an open-source bioinformatic pipeline (nf-core-oncoseq) enabling on-the-fly analysis during sequencing. We compared the AS-WGS results to those obtained by standard clinical assays, including exome and transcriptome sequencing. Results AS-WGS achieved somatic-grade coverage (mean 172X) in target regions while maintaining pan-genomic coverage (18X), thus supporting genome-wide copy number and methylation analyses. AS-WGS reliably detected all classes of clinically actionable alterations including fusion genes (20/20), small variants (SNVs and indels, in 58/59 mutated genes) and large CNVs (20/21). SNVs were robustly captured down to a 5% allelic frequency, similar to clinical exome sequencing. The PCR-free workflow supported methylation-based tumor classification, providing orthogonal confirmation of hematological and solid tumor subtypes in 9/11 acute lymphoblastic leukemias and in 8/12 solid tumors. All clonal alterations were identified with >5 supporting reads from data generated in the first 24 hours of sequencing (20/20 fusions and 47/47 SNVs with allelic frequencies > 25%), with some, such as large CNVs and methylation predictions, detected within the first hour. Conclusions Our results show that applying AS-WGS to pediatric hematological and solid tumors supports the rapid identification of all classes of genomic alterations and enables methylation-based classification in a single assay. Future efforts aimed at clinical translation will establish its position within the current multi-assay diagnostic landscape.

papers.abstract: Head and neck cancer (HNC) imposes a substantial burden in Aotearoa New Zealand (AoNZ), yet contemporary population-level data on incidence and early mortality across sociodemographic groups remain limited. This population-based retrospective cohort study used New Zealand Cancer Registry to identify all primary HNC diagnoses from 2009 to 2020 (n = 6980). The cases were classified according to ICD-10 subsites. Incidence rates (IRs), age-standardised IRs, and age-standardised rate ratios were estimated by age, sex, ethnicity, socioeconomic deprivation, and rurality. Regression models were used to estimate annual percentage change in IRs and to estimate adjusted risk ratios for two-year all-cause mortality. In total 6980 people were diagnosed with HNC; an overall incidence rate of 13.5 per 100,000 person-years (PY). Oropharyngeal cancer (OPC), the most common subsite, increased from 3.4 per 100,000 PY in 2009-2011-4.9 per 100,000 PY in 2018-2020, whereas IRs for oral cavity cancer (OCC), the second most common, were more stable. HNC IRs were higher among males, older adults, Māori, Pacific Peoples and people living in the most socioeconomically deprived areas, with subsite-specific differences: Māori experienced higher OPC incidence rates, while Pacific Peoples experienced higher OCC IRs. Within two years of diagnosis, 25.2% of patients had died. Two-year all-cause mortality was 44.4% for hypopharyngeal cancer, 30.9% for OCC, and 22.7% for OPC. Among people diagnosed with HNC, after adjusting for available sociodemographic factors and treatment timing, two-year all-cause mortality was higher for Māori, Pacific Peoples, and those in the most deprived quintile. Rurality showed no consistent association with incidence or two-year mortality. These findings indicate an OPC-driven shift in HNC epidemiology in AoNZ and a persistent inequitable burden of both disease occurrence and early mortality, supporting stronger surveillance and equity-focused cancer-control responses.
